title: Arm’s length test
learn: How a database search is screened down to true comparables
Why margins are weighted by cost, and how the percentiles are counted
What a year-end true-up is, and how it is sized
do: Screen 15 companies from a database search
Work out the margins and the arm’s length range
Test the client’s margin and draft the true-up mail

case.role: First-year article assistant, borrowed by the transfer pricing team
case.client: Brandhof Engineering Services India Private Limited, Hinjewadi, Pune: embedded software and engineering design for its Dutch parent, Brandhof Systems B.V., paid at cost plus 12%
case.team: Gayathri Sundaram (Transfer Pricing Lead); Varun Shetty, second-year article, your buddy; at Brandhof India, Smita Kale (Finance Controller)
case.goal: Before the books close, check whether Brandhof India’s margin for the year will be at arm’s length, and what true-up it needs if not.
case.where: Transfer pricing desk, Prabhat Road office · Monday 22 February 2027

messages: Brandhof India’s year-end check. The database search is back with 15 companies: screen them on my memo, then the margins and this year’s range.
Test Brandhof’s projected margin against it and draft my mail to Smita. If they need a true-up invoice, Smita has to raise it before 31 March. Draft to me by Thursday, please.

documents.title: Gayathri’s benchmark memo
documents.subject: Brandhof India: year-end check, tax year 2026–27
body: Brandhof India is tested under the transactional net margin method (TNMM): its margin on cost against independent companies doing the same kind of work. Read this before you screen.
## Our screens (the team’s, the same as in last year’s study)

1. Does different work: reject companies that sell their own products or licences, or run BPO, call-centre or data-processing work. Brandhof India writes software and does design work to its parent’s orders and owns no IP.
2. Related-party transactions above 25% of operating revenue in 2025–26: reject.
3. Operating losses in two or more of the three years 2023–24 to 2025–26: reject.
4. A financial year that does not end on 31 March: reject.
5. Operating revenue outside ₹1 crore to ₹200 crore in 2025–26: reject.
Nothing else rejects a company. Never its margin, high or low.
## Years

The comparables’ 2026–27 accounts are not out yet, so the check uses each company’s two latest years, 2024–25 and 2025–26, the years the rules fall back on when current-year accounts are not available. The October study tests the year again on 2026–27 figures where filed.
## Margin on cost (OP/OC)
- Operating profit = operating revenue less operating cost. Operating cost includes depreciation. Finance cost and other income (interest on deposits and the like) stay out.

- A company’s margin = its total operating profit for the two years ÷ its total operating cost for the two years. Rule 81 weights the years by the base of the margin, here cost, so never average the two percentages.
- Percentages to two decimals.
## The range (Income-tax Rules, 2026, rule 81)
- Put the margins in ascending order.

- Place = number of companies × 35% (65% for the top of the range, 50% for the median). Not a whole number: take the value at the next place up. A whole number: take the average of the value at that place and the next.
- With six or more companies, a margin inside the 35th to 65th percentile range is at arm’s length. Outside it, the median is the arm’s length margin.
## Year-end true-up
- Outside the range, we advise a true-up invoice to Brandhof Systems before 31 March that brings the year to the median, not to the edge of the range, which the October figures may move.
- True-up = median × operating cost, less operating profit.

documents.title: Services agreement · clause 4
documents.letterhead: Engineering Services Agreement between Brandhof Systems B.V. (the Company) and Brandhof Engineering Services India Private Limited (the Service Provider)
documents.subject: Clause 4 · Service fee
body: 4.1 For the Services, the Company shall pay the Service Provider a monthly Service Fee equal to the Cost Base for the month plus a mark-up of twelve per cent (12%).

4.2 Cost Base means all costs incurred by the Service Provider in providing the Services, as recorded in its books, excluding (a) depreciation on equipment bought out of capital contributed by the Company, and (b) interest and other finance costs.
4.3 The Service Provider shall invoice the Service Fee in Indian rupees by the 7th of the following month, on the basis of its cost-centre report. The Company shall pay within 30 days of the invoice.
4.4 Before the end of each financial year the Parties shall review the Service Fee and may agree an adjustment so that the year’s fee remains at arm’s length.

tasks.title: Screen the 15 companies

tasks.title: Work out the margins
tasks.prompt: Gayathri has your screen. Five of the nine she kept were in last year’s set and are done on her sheet. Work out the margin on cost of the four new ones over their two years, and Brandhof India’s own margin for 2026–27 from the projection. Percentages to two decimals.

lockOnLeave.note: You can’t change them after this.
lockOnLeave.done: Handed to Gayathri. You can read your margins but not change them.

hints: Add a company’s operating profit for the two years, add its operating cost for the two years, then divide. Do not average the two percentages.
For Brandhof, operating profit is revenue from operations less all four expenses. The deposit interest is other income, and depreciation stays in the cost.

notes.r1.m: Averaging 11.72% and 12.57% gives 12.15%. Two hundredths look small until Dakshin turns out to be the 35th percentile.
notes.r2.m: Its two years average 12.70%, but 2025–26, the weaker year, also had the bigger cost, so the weighted figure comes out lower.
notes.r3.m: Averaging 13.10% and 14.03% gives 13.57%. Total profit over total cost, every time: that is how the rule weights the years.
notes.r4.m: Averaging 10.57% and 12.55% gives 11.56%, which is not the rule: 2025–26, the better year, also had the bigger cost, so it counts for more.
notes.r5.m: With the deposit interest in it reads 12.32%, and on the billed cost of 6,534 it reads 12.00%. Neither is the margin the comparables are measured on.

tasks.title: Build the range and test Brandhof
tasks.prompt: Gayathri’s checked sheet has all nine margins. Build the range and the median as her memo sets out. Then two figures for Brandhof: its margin if the costs left out of the invoices were billed with the 12% mark-up, and the true-up to the median, in ₹ lakh. Percentages to two decimals.

lockOnLeave.ask: Hand your range and true-up to Gayathri?
lockOnLeave.note: You can’t change them after this.
lockOnLeave.done: Handed to Gayathri. You can read your figures but not change them.

hints: Rank the nine from lowest to highest. A place such as 3.15 is not a whole number, so take the value at the next place up, the 4th. Excel’s PERCENTILE functions interpolate between values; the rule takes the value at a place.
The left-out costs are in the P&L notes and Smita’s mail. The true-up is the median’s operating profit less the operating profit the projection shows.

v.working: 9 × 0.35 = 3.15, not a whole number: the 4th value, Dakshin

notes.p35.v: Excel’s PERCENTILE.INC gives 12.07%, between the 3rd and 4th values. The rule takes the value at the place, the 4th.
notes.p65.v: Varun’s PERCENTILE.INC gives 13.78%, a wider range than the rule allows.
notes.med.v: A whole-number place would mean the average of two values, the one there and the next; with nine companies, no place comes out whole.
notes.fix.v: Rig depreciation ₹84 lakh and Floor 7 rent ₹24 lakh: ₹108 lakh, or ₹120.96 lakh with the mark-up. Cost plus 12% on the whole cost is exactly 12.00%, and the range starts at 12.17%.
notes.tu.v: ₹120.96 lakh of it is the two costs with their mark-up; the other ₹45.17 lakh is the gap between 12% and the median.

tasks.title: Draft the mail to Smita
tasks.prompt: Gayathri sends this to Smita under her name. Pick the right line for each part of the mail: what we found, why, whether fixing the bill is enough, and what we advise. Add a line of your own if you like.
hints: Each line must hold up if Smita forwards it to her auditors: the margin on the whole cost, the real cause, and a true-up that reaches the median.

freeText.label: Your own line for the mail

model.intro: Nine of the fifteen companies pass the screens. Weighted by cost over 2024–25 and 2025–26, they give a range of 12.17% to 13.59% and a median of 12.68%. Brandhof India’s projected 10.18% is below the range: ₹108 lakh of cost never reached the invoices, and even billed at cost plus 12% the year would reach only 12.00%. A true-up of ₹166.13 lakh before 31 March brings the year to the median.

blocks.text: The nine, lowest to highest, with the places the rule counts:

Brandhof India: 676.08 ÷ 6,642.00 = 10.18%, below 12.17%. Billing the ₹108 lakh left out, with its 12%, gives 797.04 ÷ 6,642.00 = 12.00%: still below. True-up to the median: 12.68% × 6,642.00 = 842.21, less 676.08 = ₹166.13 lakh.

items: Out on their work: Akshaya (its own software licences) and Orvitas (back-office and voice work).
Out on the other filters: Sarvatra (41% with its group), Pratibimb (losses in 2023–24 and 2024–25), Meruvi (year ends 31 December) and Sutrakar (₹312 crore of revenue).
In, though they look odd: Corvanta, the highest margin of the nine, and Halasya, at 19% with related parties, under the 25% line.

blocks.text: The bill was short because clause 4.2 keeps the rigs’ depreciation out and Floor 7 never reached the template. Amend the clause and the template from April, and 12% still sits under this year’s range: the mark-up itself needs a look before the next agreement.

principles: A comparable is chosen for the work it does and the independence of its prices, never for its margin.
Weight each company’s years by its cost, rank the set, and count the places the rule’s way: a place that is not a whole number goes up to the next value.
Test the margin on the whole operating cost. What the agreement leaves out of the bill is still cost.

interview.q: What is the arm’s length price, and why is it tested?
interview.checking: Whether you can explain transfer pricing in plain words before any method.
outline: It is the price unrelated parties would agree on for the same deal in similar conditions.
Group companies could move profit between countries through their prices, so the Act tests such deals against it.
In the simulation a captive on cost plus 12% earned 10.18% on its whole cost, below the range.

interview.q: How did you build the arm’s length range?
interview.checking: Whether you know the Indian method: weighted margins, the rule’s percentiles, the median when the margin falls outside.
outline: In the simulation I screened {n} companies on work, related-party share, losses, year end and size[[, rejecting {rej}]].
Each margin was both years’ operating profit over both years’ operating cost: weighted by cost, not averaged.
Ranked, the 4th and 6th of nine gave 12.17%–13.59%; the client was below, so the median applied.
